$comment: The parameters of every tool operation. Hand-written: this is the specification, and it covers the catalogue exhaustively — `every_catalog_operation_declares_its_parameters` fails if an operation is added without an entry here. `scripts/generate-command-surface.mjs` emits the Rust table that refuses a call, the tool the model is given, and the addon-side guard for the operations the addon answers.
$commandComment: `command` is the addon command that answers the operation, and its absence — with `answeredBy: "rust"` in its place — means the operation never reaches the addon. Those are checked in Rust and deserialize into a typed request behind it; `every_rust_answered_operation_matches_its_request` holds this file to those structs.
$summaryComment: `summary` is what the model reads about the operation, one sentence, and it is the half of the tool description a person writes. One sentence because the arm that cut every summary to its first one tied on success against the shipped surface and saved a quarter of the prompt; `godot_runtime.input` is the exception, its second sentence being the one rule a live run showed the model does not already obey. It lives here rather than in Rust because everything else about the same operation already did — the parameters it takes, what answers it, where it may sit in an `ops` list, whether the user is asked first — and the worker is sent one object per operation carrying all of it. Written apart, the view the model receives was assembled at serialization time out of two files nothing held together, and a test had to read English out of Rust source to check the seam.
$acceptsComment: `accepts` names a parameter the addon reads and the model is never told about. `scene` is the only one: every node command takes it and defaults it to the scene the editor already has open, so the desktop client passes it and the model has no reason to.
$gatedComment: `gated` is the sentence the user is shown before the agent may run this operation. Its absence means auto-allowed, so a new operation is allowed by default and has to be gated deliberately. It lives beside the parameters and the route because all three are facts about the same operation, and keeping the safety model in a table of its own meant a fifth place to look and a fifth thing to hold to the catalogue afterwards.
$writesComment: `writes` names what an operation writes where one of the user's enforced Godot rules may refuse it: `projectSetting` and `editorSetting` are the two settings surfaces, `scriptText` is a call carrying GDScript source. `godot_policy::enforcement_refusal` reads the tag rather than matching on the tool and the operation, so an operation renamed here cannot quietly stop being enforced. Absence means no rule keys on this operation — which is every operation but five.
$resultComment: `result` is the shape of the answer an operation succeeds with, in the same vocabulary as `params` and never shown to the model. The generator emits a Rust struct per addon command from it, and `godot_rpc` deserializes every answer into that struct in a debug build — so a declaration that disagrees with the handler is a failed acceptance run rather than a stale sentence. A kind of `shape` names a row of `shapes` below; an `object` with no `entry` is one this codebase does not shape at all — a settings map, a language server payload — and says so by being open.
$aloneComment: `alone` narrows where an operation may sit in an `ops` list, and carries the sentence a caller reads when it gets that wrong. Every tool call is a list, so a model wanting three inspections writes one call rather than three. `scope: "repeat"` is the ordinary case: the operation may sit beside other operations, and may not appear twice, because it takes no parameters to vary or drives something the session owns exactly one of — the open scene, the running game, the undo stack, the dialog. The router runs a list in order, so a second one would only redo or undo the first. `scope: "exclusive"` is the debugger, where each answer decides what the next operation means, so the operation has to be the only entry of its call. Absence means the operation may appear as often as a list names it.
$vocabularyComment: `vocabularies` names a set of words a parameter accepts where `kind` cannot reach — `key` sits inside each entry of an `events` list — and it names them by pointing at a list in `protocol/godot-vocabulary.json`, which is written by running the pinned engine. Nothing here is hand-listed: the twenty-five key names that used to be were a quarter of the hundred and ninety the engine has, and the only thing holding them to it was a test feeding them to a real editor one at a time. The generator resolves `engine` into the words, emits them as the schema `enum` the sampler is constrained by, and the prose says nothing about them: an enum permits and prose steers, and the same enum with a stale list beside it measured worse than with none.
$domainsComment: `domains` is the ten groupings the hundred operations are offered as. It is a decision about presentation rather than a fact about an operation, which is why it is a block of its own. A domain used to carry a description as well; the arm that cut all ten tied on success, so the model reads the domain's name and its operations and nothing else. `ai_tools.rs` CATALOG is generated from this, in this order.

operations.summary: Injects input and captures the result. Each event names its kind and the parameters that kind uses, as {"kind": "key", "key": "A", "pressed": true} — send the release as a second event, or the key stays down. An event that leaves `pressed` out alternates on its own: the first is the press and the second the release, so a click is the same event written twice. A Button answers the release, not the press. A mouse_button event names its `button`, a joypad_button event its `joypadButton`, and a joypad_motion event its `axis`. A position is [x, y]. This drives the Input Map, so it is how you check that a level you built can actually be played. Its answer carries a frame, unless a later entry of the same call carries one too: a picture another picture replaces is not worth sending, and a moment in the middle of a key sequence is what capture is for.
